Sharp conditioning and quantitative stability of optimal transport

Yuanlong Ruan Address: Beihang University, Beijing, China
Date: October 6, 2026
Abstract.

When a feasible plan is obtained whose quadratic transport cost is known to be close to the optimal cost, we try to determine how close the feasible plan is to the true optimal map under mild density and moment conditions. The source and target may be unbounded or have non-compact supports. We show that for a source with density in LpL^{p} and an nn-th moment, let s=1−1/ps=1-1/p and η=s​n/[n+(d−1)​s]\eta=sn/[n+(d-1)s]. Under the target constraint ∫|y|m​[log⁡(e+|y|)]β​𝑑ν⩽1\int|y|^{m}[\log(e+|y|)]^{\beta}\,d\nu\leqslant 1, the worst-case class-uniform conditioning has a sharp modulus comparable to

tη⁡(m−2)/[m⁡(1+η)−η][log(e/t)]−β(2+η)/[m(1+η)−η],t^{\eta(m-2)/[m(1+\eta)-\eta]}[\log(e/t)]^{-\beta(2+\eta)/[m(1+\eta)-\eta]},

whenever t>0t>0 is small. This holds for m⩾2m\geqslant 2 and β⩾0\beta\geqslant 0. When m=2m=2, every β>0\beta>0 gives a sharp logarithmic modulus, whereas the m=2,β=0m=2,\,\beta=0 extreme has no vanishing modulus. The matching lower bound is verified for both the squared map error and barycentric projection error. The sharp map error bounds allow us to directly derive quantitative stabilities of common source Brenier maps without passing through potential estimates, thereby avoiding loss of information. These stabilities strictly improve the corresponding results of Delalande-Merigot [13] and Letrouit-Mérigot [19] under identical or weaker settings, particularly no convexity of the source support or bounds of the source density are assumed.

Key words and phrases: 
optimal transport, quantitative stability, power-logarithm conditioning, sharp error bound, non-compact support

1. Introduction and main results

Quantitative stability of optimal transport has attracted a substantial effort in the literature with seminal works [6, 22, 13, 10, 23] and in Wasserstein barycenter stability [9, 11]. The settings are mostly for compactly supported source, convex source support or a combination of the two. Unbounded source support is considered recently, e.g., [20], which also extends the strong convexity theory of [13] to more general domains. Sources are treated through variance inequalities and gluing. Extension to general cost [24] is also studied. If more regularities are assumed, stronger stabilities are anticipated. For example [18] assumes strong cc-concavity with general costs, [4] treats smooth map stability and statistical consequences, [8] proves Lipschitz stability for nondegenerate Hölder densities on smooth uniformly convex domains, to name a few.

Our focus in this article is to provide a matched conditioning law under simultaneous density and moment constraints and its power-logarithm case, including rough and singlar targets. It is designed to answer the question: if an approximate feasible plan is obtained whose transport cost is known to be close to the ground true within a given tolerance and an approximate optimal map is constructed, then what we can say about how close the constructed map is to the true optimal map? The answer to this question will have its own numerical benefits, but it will also allow us to treat the quantitative stability of optimal transport maps without touching the potentials. As implied by the recent work [23], we believe going from potential to map could cause loss of information if the goal is stability of Brenier map itself.

The first quantity OPEN(Equation 1.1CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:Eintro}}}\right), the squared map error, measures the error of the plan σ\sigma relative to the map TνT_{\nu} at the same source point. The second quantity OPEN𝒟ν​(σCLOSE)\mathcal{D}_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma}}\right) is the objective/cost gap, the difference between the cost of an approximate plan σ\sigma and the optimal cost OPEN12​W22​(ρ,νCLOSE)\frac{1}{2}W_{2}^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\rho,\nu}}\right).

A general plan σ\sigma may split mass. Barycentric projection [3, Definition 5.4.2][25] is the usual way to reconstruct an approximate map. Write σ(d​x,d​yCLOSE)=ρ(d​xCLOSE)σx(d​yCLOSE)\sigma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(dx,dy}}\right)=\rho\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(dx}}\right)\sigma_{x}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(dy}}\right), where σx\sigma_{x} is the conditional kernel. The barycentric projection is defined for ρ\rho-a.e. x,x,

OPENOPENT¯σ​(xCLOSE)=∫y​d​σx​(yCLOSE).\bar{T}_{\sigma}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)=\int yd\sigma_{x}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right).

If we write

Vσ=∫|y−T¯σ(xCLOSE)|2dσ(x,yCLOSE),V_{\sigma}=\int\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|y-\bar{T}_{\sigma}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right|^{2}d\sigma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right),

then

(1.4) ℰν(σCLOSE)=‖T¯σ−Tν‖OPENL2​(ρCLOSE)2+Vσ.\mathcal{E}_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\bar{T}_{\sigma}-T_{\nu}}}\right\|_{L^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\rho}}\right)}^{2}+V_{\sigma}.

The cross term vanishes because OPENOPEN∫(y−T¯σ​(xCLOSE))​d​σx​(yCLOSE)=0\int\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y-\bar{T}_{\sigma}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)d\sigma_{x}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)=0. The barycentric map T¯σ\bar{T}_{\sigma} needs not push ρ\rho to ν\nu.

We ask how accurately a small objective gap determines the optimal map, uniformly over a specified class of marginals. This is a quantitative stability question in practice: does a nearly optimal feasible plan approximate the optimal map, and at what rate?

There are two aspects of this question. The first is conditioning which views the question as the conversion of objective gap into squared map error, i.e. a bound of the form

𝒟ν(σCLOSE)⩽t⟹ℰν(σCLOSE)⩽ω(tCLOSE),\mathcal{D}_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma}}\right)\leqslant t\implies\mathcal{E}_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma}}\right)\leqslant\omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right),

where ω\omega is a conditioning modulus. Its size measures how much map error a given objective tolerance permits under required assumptions. It provides a sufficient upper error modulus. For a fixed class 𝒞\mathcal{C} of probability marginals, define

(1.5) Ω𝒞(tCLOSE)={ℰν(σCLOSE):(ρ,νCLOSE)∈𝒞, σ∈Π(ρ,νCLOSE), 𝒟ν(σCLOSE)⩽t}.\Omega_{\mathcal{C}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathcal{E}_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma}}\right):\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\rho,\nu}}\right)\in\mathcal{C},\text{ }\sigma\in\Pi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\rho,\nu}}\right),\text{ }\mathcal{D}_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma}}\right)\leqslant t}}\right\}.

This is the smallest class-uniform conditioning modulus. An upper bound OPENOPENΩ𝒞​(tCLOSE)⩽C​φ​(tCLOSE)\Omega_{\mathcal{C}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right)\leqslant C\varphi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right) answers how small a cost tolerance is sufficient for desired solution accuracy. A matching lower bound OPENOPENΩ𝒞​(tCLOSE)⩾c​φ​(tCLOSE)\Omega_{\mathcal{C}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right)\geqslant c\varphi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right) answers whether a uniformly better conversion can follow from the same requirement. Together they describe the intrinsic worst-case information provided by the cost gap. This is a class-uniform stability, OPENΩ𝒞​(tCLOSE)→0\Omega_{\mathcal{C}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right)\rightarrow 0 as t→0.t\rightarrow 0. By OPEN(Equation 1.4CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:variance-decomposition}}}\right), it also justifies the barycentric reconstruction.

The other aspect is data perturbation: how does the optimal map change when a marginal changes? The two aspects are closedly related but not the same. Uniform stability implies indivisual stability, but the converse does not hold. Failure of uniform stability does not rule out stability for a fixed pair of marginals.

1.2. Main results and organization

The structural distribution-adaptive estimate. Under the Brenier setting of Assumption 1, Section section 5 proves the structural estimate for an arbitrary plan OPENσ∈Π​(ρ,νCLOSE),\sigma\in\Pi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\rho,\nu}}\right),

(1.6) ℰν(σ)⩽infb∈ℝd,R,h>0{4R𝒟ν​(σ)h+18R2𝔄ρ(h)+8τ2,ν,b(R)}.\mathcal{E}_{\nu}(\sigma)\leqslant\inf_{b\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\,R,h>0}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{4R\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\nu}(\sigma)}{h}+18R^{2}\mathfrak{A}_{\rho}(h)+8\tau_{2,\nu,b}(R)}}\right\}.

Here 𝔄ρ\mathfrak{A}_{\rho} measures squared subgradient oscillation of convex 11-Lipschitz functions and τ2,ν,b\tau_{2,\nu,b} is the ordinary squared target tail. The information of the source measure enters only 𝔄ρ\mathfrak{A}_{\rho} and is processed through the elegent geometric estimates from [12, 9]. The estimate is also inspired by the recent work [23]. One advantage of the structural estimate is it allows us to treat source and target separately, giving distribution-adaptive error bound. Moreover, since we directly addresss the stability of the maps, more information is retained. Definitions and concrete controls appear in Sections section 3 - section 6.

Source estimates and power laws. Under appropriate source density conditions, ρ=f​d​x,\rho=fdx, OPENf∈Lp​(ℝdCLOSE),f\in L^{p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}}}\right), 1<p⩽∞1<p\leqslant\infty and s=1−1/p,s=1-1/p, Theorem Theorem 2 and Theorem Theorem 3 combine subgradient oscillation estimates with an mm-th target moment, m>2m>2 to build power laws for ℰν​(σ).\mathcal{E}_{\nu}(\sigma). For bounded densities and compact source and target, Corollary Corollary 1 gives

ℰν(σ)⩽Const⋅𝒟ν(σ)OPENs/(1+sCLOSE), 0<s⩽1.\mathcal{E}_{\nu}(\sigma)\leqslant\operatorname*{Const}\cdot\mathcal{D}_{\nu}(\sigma)^{s/\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+s}}\right)},\text{ }0<s\leqslant 1.

When p=∞p=\infty, s=1,s=1, this is the squared map error estimate of Mérigot [23, Theorem 3.4 (3.15)], for an arbitrary feasible plan with the same marginals as the reference optimal map. The correlation gap there equals OPEN(Equation 1.2CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:Dintro}}}\right). The constructions in Section section 9 confirms that a matching class-uniform modulus is not available in the extreme cases, including the unbounded density and m=2m=2 cases. For a prescribed L1L^{1} density the source profile still vanishes.

The power-logarithm conditioning law. The pure power law is established in Theorem Theorem 3 with a matching lower bound verified in Theorem Theorem 6, and consolidated in Theorem Theorem 7 when m⩾2,m\geqslant 2, β=0.\beta=0. With

η=s​nn+(d−1)​s, H=m(1+η)−η,\eta=\frac{sn}{n+(d-1)s},\text{ }H=m(1+\eta)-\eta,

the pure power law is, for small t>0,t>0,

OPENΩ𝒞m,0​(tCLOSE)≃tOPENη​(m−1CLOSE)/H,\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{m,0}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right)\simeq t^{\eta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m-1}}\right)/H},

for the fixed class 𝒞m,0\mathcal{C}_{m,0} defined in Section section 10. Theorem Theorem 7 in Section section 10 extends it to the logarithmically weighted target moment class 𝒞m,β,\mathcal{C}_{m,\beta}, giving the power-logarithm law

Ω𝒞m,β(tCLOSE)≃tOPENη​(m−1CLOSE)/H[log(e/tCLOSE)]OPEN−β​(2+ηCLOSE)/H.\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{m,\beta}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right)\simeq t^{\eta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m-1}}\right)/H}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e/t}}\right)}}\right]^{-\beta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2+\eta}}\right)/H}.

Brenier map stabilities with common source. Section section 11 introduces a repairing process that constructs an optimal plan through a coupling of two targets. The objective gap of the repaired plan is then controlled by centered source moments or integrated source tails.

For compact source and target, Theorem Theorem 8 gives

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)⩽Const⋅W1​(μ,ν)s/[2​(1+s)].\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leqslant\operatorname*{Const}\cdot W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{s/[2(1+s)]}.

At p=∞p=\infty, s=1,s=1, this recovers Mérigot’s 1/41/4 power [23, Theorem 3.1]. It is also the common source specialization of [17, Theorem 4.6]. Here the error is an L2L^{2} norm, not its square, and the input is the distance between two targets, not a feasible plan’s cost gap. The passage between these problems requires the repairing argument in the proof of Theorem Theorem 8, not just taking a square root.

Theorem Theorem 11 gives the corresponding map bound for unbounded non-compact sources and targets under its stated moment assumptions,

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)⩽Const⋅W1​(μ,ν)α​Θη,m/2.\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leqslant\operatorname*{Const}\cdot W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\alpha\Theta_{\eta,m}/2}.

And in Section subsection 12.1, we discuss the sharpness of the exponent.

The flexible structural estimate OPEN(Equation 1.6CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:error-intro}}}\right) permits the combinations of various source and target assumptions, each combination may lead to a dedicated quantiative stability which exploits specific properties of a given family of marginals thus gives stronger stability than the general theorem would provide, and the sharp conditioning can also give refined stability. But we have refrained from exhausting the combinations and focus instead on combinations of moments and compactness of supports.

Section Appendix A, Section Appendix B, Section Appendix C are devoted to comparisons, particularly showing dedicated quantiative stabilities for specific probability classes. These sections may be read as applications of the main results. The main part of the article does not depend on these materials.

Further comparisons with prior works and strict improvements. For targets in a fixed ball and δ=W1​(μ,ν)\delta=W_{1}(\mu,\nu), we prove in Section subsection B.1, for source with Gaussian upper envelope (Theorem Theorem 14), such as the log-concave family, that

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)⩽Const⋅δ1/4[log(c/δCLOSE)]1/8, if f(xCLOSE)⩽C0e−κ|x−a|2/2,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}}}\right\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leqslant\operatorname*{Const}\cdot\delta^{1/4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(c/\delta}}\right)}}\right]^{1/8},\text{ \ if }f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\leqslant C_{0}e^{-\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x-a}}\right|^{2}/2},

and for source with polynomial upper envelope (Theorem Theorem 15), that

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)⩽Const⋅δOPENOPEN(β−d−1CLOSE)/(4​(β−dCLOSE)), if f(xCLOSE)⩽C0(1+|x−a|2)−β/2, β>d+2.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}}}\right\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leqslant\operatorname*{Const}\cdot\delta^{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta-d-1}}\right)/\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(4\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta-d}}\right)}}\right)},\text{ \ if }f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\leqslant C_{0}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x-a}}\right|^{2}}}\right)^{-\beta/2},\text{ }\beta>d+2.

On common hypotheses these improve the map exponents in [19, Theorems 1.4 and 1.12]. The first also avoids an upper Hessian bound, and the second avoids a density lower bound. Precise comparisons are given after the corresponding proofs.

Section Appendix A gives detailed comparison with [13, Section 4] on Brenier map stability between compact source and noncompact target. Section Appendix B is devoted to comparison with the corresponding results of [19] on compact source and target under various source density assumptions. Our Brenier map stability results give strict improvements in all these comparisons under identical or weaker assumptions.

From objective gap to reconstructed maps. Section Appendix C is for applications. It treats the verification of solution accuracy from primal-dual gap, and gives barycentric map error bounds under explicit accuracy requirements. It is worth noting in passing that the map error bound and the conditioning law could also be used in regularized settings, such as verification of the accuracy of entropic map [26], or barycentric map constructed from divergence-regularized optimal transport plan [14]. The theory will tell us when to stop a solver to reach a desired solution accuracy.

Remark 1.

Throughout the article, when compactly supported probability measures are defined, we use closed balls such as 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁B​(a,RX𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸),B\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(a,R_{X}}}\right), 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁B​(b,RY𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)B\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(b,R_{Y}}}\right) to indicate where their supports belong. But no convexity of these underlying sets are needed.

2.2. Transport, potentials and integrability

The following is the standing assumption that holds throughout the paper.

Assumption 1 (Brenier setting).

The Borel probability measures ρ,\rho, ν\nu belong to 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁𝒫2​(ℝd𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)\mathcal{P}_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}}}\right). There is a proper lower semicontinuous convex function u:ℝd↦(−∞,+∞𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸]u:\mathbb{R}^{d}\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-\infty,+\infty}}\right] such that the unique optimal plan from ρ\rho to ν\nu is 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁(Id,T𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)#​ρ\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\operatorname{Id},T}}\right)_{\#}\rho, where T=∇u,T=\nabla u, ρ\rho-a.e. The potential is chosen so that

u∈L1(ρCLOSE), u∗∈L1(νCLOSE).u\in L^{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\rho}}\right),\text{ }u^{\ast}\in L^{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\nu}}\right).

If ρ≪d​x\rho\ll dx, this assumption follows from Brenier’s theorem and quadratic Kantorovich duality [7, 30, 29]. Some singular sources are also admissible if they do not give mass to small sets of Hausdorff dimension at most d−1d-1, but we retain Assumption 1 whenever singular sources are discussed [21].

In general for a proper convex u,u, dom∂u⊂domu\operatorname{dom}\partial u\subset\operatorname{dom}u [27, Theorems 23.4]. Assumption 1 implies that

(2.1) ρ(x:∂u(xCLOSE)={∇u})=ρ(dom∂u)=ρ(dom⁡uCLOSE)=1.\rho\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x:\partial u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\nabla u}}\right\}}}\right)=\rho\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\operatorname{dom}\partial u}}\right)=\rho\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\operatorname{dom}u}}\right)=1.

For a lower semicontinuous convex v:ℝd↦(−∞,+∞CLOSE]v:\mathbb{R}^{d}\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-\infty,+\infty}}\right], its conjugate and subdifferential are

Let v:ℝd↦ℝv:\mathbb{R}^{d}\mapsto\mathbb{R} be convex. For h>0h>0, define its subgradient oscillation around a point xx by

In particular it is Borel measurable.

4. The proximal Fenchel estimate

In the proof of Theorem Theorem 1 we will need a local slope with required closeness to a given subgradient. The proximal map produces such a slope. For λ>0\lambda>0, define

proxλ​u(ξCLOSE)≜argminz∈ℝd{u(zCLOSE)+|z−ξ|22​λ}.\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda u}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\xi}}\right)\triangleq\arg\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z}}\right)+\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z-\xi}}\right|^{2}}{2\lambda}}}\right\}.

The proximal operator is well-defined for proper lower semicontinuous convex uu with unique minimizer for each ξ.\xi. The first order condition of the minimization gives

0∈∂[u(zCLOSE)+|z−ξ|22​λ].0\in\partial\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z}}\right)+\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z-\xi}}\right|^{2}}{2\lambda}}}\right].

The two terms have non-empty intersection of domain relative interiors, since the quadratic term has a domain relative interior of ℝd.\mathbb{R}^{d}. So

0∈∂u(zCLOSE)+z−ξλ or equivalently ξ−zλ∈∂u(zCLOSE).0\in\partial u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z}}\right)+\frac{z-\xi}{\lambda}\text{ or equivalently }\frac{\xi-z}{\lambda}\in\partial u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z}}\right).

We recall a useful property of the proximal map OPENproxλ​u⁡(⋅CLOSE)\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda u}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\cdot}}\right) that it is nonexpansive. Indeed, if OPENzi=proxλ​u⁡(ξiCLOSE)z_{i}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda u}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\xi_{i}}}\right), i=1,2,i=1,2, set

OPENqi=ξi−ziλ∈∂u⁡(ziCLOSE).q_{i}=\frac{\xi_{i}-z_{i}}{\lambda}\in\partial u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z_{i}}}\right).

Then by the cyclic monotonicity of the subdifferential we have OPENOPEN(q1−q2CLOSE)⋅(z1−z2CLOSE)⩾0\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(q_{1}-q_{2}}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right)\geqslant 0, and hence

|z1−z2|2=(ξ1−ξ2CLOSE)⋅(z1−z2CLOSE)−λ(q1−q2CLOSE)⋅(z1−z2CLOSE)⩽|ξ1−ξ2||z1−z2|.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right|^{2}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\xi_{1}-\xi_{2}}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right)-\lambda\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(q_{1}-q_{2}}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right)\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|\xi_{1}-\xi_{2}}}\right|\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right|.

If |z1−z2|\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right| is not zero, we obtain

|z1−z2|⩽|ξ1−ξ2|.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right|\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|\xi_{1}-\xi_{2}}}\right|.

When |z1−z2|=0,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z_{1}-z_{2}}}\right|=0, the inequality is trivial. Therefore nonexpansiveness follows.

The next construction gives the local slope that we need later. The estimate OPEN(Equation 4.5CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:prox-gap}}}\right), which is a kind of coercivity of the Fenchel gap OPEN(Equation 4.5CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:prox-gap}}}\right), is proved in [12, Lemma 1.1].

Lemma 3 (Pointwise proximal estimate).

Let uu be proper lower semicontinuous and convex. For fixed x,x, x′∈dom∂u,x^{\prime}\in\operatorname*{dom}\partial u, suppose that 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁p∈∂u​(x𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)p\in\partial u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right), 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁r∈∂u​(x′𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)r\in\partial u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x^{\prime}}}\right), and |p|,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|p}}\right|, |r|⩽R\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|r}}\right|\leqslant R. For λ>0\lambda>0, define

(4.1) z=proxλ​u(x+λ​rCLOSE), v=r+x−zλ.z=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda u}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x+\lambda r}}\right),\text{ }v=r+\frac{x-z}{\lambda}.

Then

(4.2) OPENv∈∂u​(zCLOSE),v\in\partial u\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z}}\right),
(4.3) |z−x|⩽2Rλ,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|z-x}}\right|\leqslant 2R\lambda,
(4.4) |v|⩽3R,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|v}}\right|\leqslant 3R,
(4.5) gu(x,rCLOSE)⩾λ|v−r|2.g_{u}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,r}}\right)\geqslant\lambda\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|v-r}}\right|^{2}.

The inclusion OPEN(Equation 4.2CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:prox-subgrad}}}\right) follows from the first-order condition

The next is a simple way to truncate long-distance transports which we call a slope-clipping principle. For convex functions, it has appeared in [10, 23]. See also [15] for general handling.

The next theorem is the structural result of the paper. It turns the Fenchel gap into a map error bound by separating three contributions: the objective gap, the source mass near convex singularities and target tail.

Remark 3.

Note that the compactness of the source is not used in the proof. It enters only in some estimates of 𝔄ρ\mathfrak{A}_{\rho}, thus allowing us to treat source and target tails separately.

9. Sharpness and extreme cases

The section tries to determine the sharpness of the exponents of the error bound obtained in the preceding section. Here the sharpness means with a given class of probability marginals, the exponent cannot be increased uniformly for all pairs of marginals in that class.

9.1. Sharpness of Theorem Theorem 2

The next theorem establishes sharpness of the map error exponent in Theorem Theorem 2. The example below does not uniformly satisfy the strong assumptions of Corollary Corollary 1, there is no common bounded target support as h→0h\rightarrow 0.

We now provide the stability of Brenier map for compact source and target with moment. Since it will used later, we will give a version that slightly weakens the target moment condition to squared tail control. The tail radius cutoff is set to 11 to only look at the the tail for measures that might have singularities near the origin. A probability measure with β\beta-th moment implies the tail bound, but not the reverse. The tail bound controls behaviour near infinity.

12.1. Sharpness of Theorem Theorem 11 in dimension one

The sharp error bound exponent in Theorem Theorem 3 does not necessarily make the exponent for the Brenier map bound OPEN(Equation 12.5CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:both-unbounded}}}\right) of Theorem Theorem 11 sharp, although the latter is indeed sharp for compact source and target proved in Theorem Theorem 8. In dimension one the exponent is in fact strictly suboptimal, as the following shows.

Let d=1d=1. Recall that for any probability measure η\eta on ℝ\mathbb{R}, the distribution function and its quantile function are given by

Fη(x)=η((−∞,x]), Gη(t)=inf{x∈ℝ:Fη(x)⩾t}, 0<t<1.F_{\eta}(x)=\eta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(({-\infty},x]}}\right),\text{ }G_{\eta}(t)=\inf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}:F_{\eta}(x)\geqslant t}}\right\},\text{ }0<t<1.

{t:Gη(t)>x}=(Fη​(x),1CLOSE).\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{t:G_{\eta}(t)>x}}\right\}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(F_{\eta}(x),1}}\right).

Appendix B Comparisons with Letrouit-Mérigot [19]

We now compare with the Brenier map stability estimates [19, Theorem 1.4 (1.7), Theorem 1.7 (1.10), Theorem 1.10 (1.13), Theorem 1.11 (1.15) and Theorem 1.12 (1.17)]. As already mentioned in its Remark 1.5, these stabilities are extendible to non-compact targets under additional moments via the route of [13, Section 4]. For comparison purpose we only treat compact targets, non-compact targets can be treated as in Theorem Theorem 10 or Theorem Theorem 11. Therefore we assume that throughout this section, the targets μ,\mu, ν\nu lie in one fixed common ball B⁡(b,RY)B(b,R_{Y}), RY>0R_{Y}>0, and δ=W1​(μ,ν)\delta=W_{1}(\mu,\nu).

Appendix C From objective gap to map accuracy

Dual-based algorithms for optimal transport usually use primal-dual gap as stopping criterion. An approximate optimal map is then constructed, e.g., through barycentric projection. The purpose of this section is to demonstrate turning a primal-dual gap into an error bound for barycentric projection map. Let Ψρ,ν​(z)\Psi_{\rho,\nu}(z) denote the infimum on the right of OPEN(Equation 5.1CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:error-bound}}}\right), with objective gap replaced by z⩾0z\geqslant 0. It is nondecreasing, since every expression being minimized is nondecreasing.

Corollary 4.

Fix ρ,ν\rho,\nu satisfying Assumption 1, a plan σ∈Π⁡(ρ,ν)\sigma\in\Pi(\rho,\nu), and integrable functions ϕ∈L1​(ρ)\phi\in L^{1}(\rho), ψ∈L1​(ν)\psi\in L^{1}(\nu) such that ϕ(x)+ψ(y)⩽|x−y|2/2\phi(x)+\psi(y)\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x-y}}\right|^{2}/2 for every x,yx,y. Let

ϵ=12​∫|x−y|2​𝑑σ−∫ϕ​𝑑ρ−∫ψ​𝑑ν\epsilon=\frac{1}{2}\int|x-y|^{2}\,d\sigma-\int\phi\,d\rho-\int\psi\,d\nu

be the primal-dual gap. Then 0⩽𝒟ν​(σ)⩽ϵ0\leqslant\mathcal{D}_{\nu}(\sigma)\leqslant\epsilon and

‖T¯σ−Tν‖22+Vσ=ℰν(σCLOSE)⩽Ψρ,ν(ϵCLOSE).\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\bar{T}_{\sigma}-T_{\nu}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}+V_{\sigma}=\mathcal{E}_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma}}\right)\leqslant\Psi_{\rho,\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\epsilon}}\right).

It is a result of Theorem Theorem 1, the monotonicity of Ψρ,ν\Psi_{\rho,\nu} and OPEN(Equation 1.4CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\autoref{eq:variance-decomposition}}}\right). ∎
